learn.title: 1 — Davis: Engineering as a Profession
learn.body:
Michael Davis's 1995 article traces how engineering became a recognized profession in the 19th century. Davis argues that a profession is distinguished not just by technical expertise but by a code of conduct — shared ethical standards members are expected to follow.

Before the mid-19th century, builders and mechanics did much of what we now call engineering without formal credentials or organized professional bodies. The emergence of professional engineering societies (like the ASCE, founded 1852) and later engineering ethics codes transformed engineering into a profession in the modern sense.

learn.title: 2 — Engineering vs. Science
learn.body:
A central theme in both readings is the distinction between engineering and science. Science seeks to understand how nature works; engineering seeks to change the world by applying knowledge to build things. Scientists ask "why?"; engineers ask "how do we make this work?"

Henry Petroski's short essay "Scientists vs. Engineers" captures this tension. He notes that scientists and engineers are trained differently, value different things, and often misunderstand each other. Scientists prize publication and peer recognition; engineers value things that work.

learn.title: 3 — Engineering vs. Technology
learn.body:
Technology is a broader term than engineering — it includes all the tools, machines, techniques, and knowledge systems humans have developed. Engineering is a particular, formalized practice within technology: applying scientific principles using mathematical analysis within economic and social constraints.

Not all technology is engineered — traditional crafts, vernacular architecture, and folk medicine are all technology without formal engineering. Conversely, modern engineering always involves technology but is characterized by its reliance on systematic knowledge and professional standards.

learn.title: 4 — Engineering as Professional Practice
learn.body:
Davis emphasizes that engineering is not just technical skill but a social practice embedded in institutions, norms, and ethical commitments. The professional engineer operates within a web of obligations: to employers, to clients, to the public, and to the profession itself.

This multiplicity of obligations creates potential conflicts of interest — for example, when an employer wants something that raises public safety risks. Understanding engineering historically helps clarify how these obligations arose and how engineers have navigated (or failed to navigate) them — groundwork for the ethics cases in Section 3.

anki.q: What is Michael Davis's main argument in 'An Historical Preface to Engineering Ethics'?
anki.a: Engineering became a profession in the 19th century through the development of shared ethical standards and codes of conduct — not just technical expertise.

anki.q: What distinguishes a 'profession' from other kinds of work, according to Davis?
anki.a: A profession has a shared code of conduct (ethical standards) that members are expected to follow, beyond mere technical competence.

anki.q: When was the ASCE founded and why is it significant?
anki.a: 1852 — one of the first professional engineering societies, helping formalize engineering as a recognized profession.

anki.q: What is the key difference between science and engineering?
anki.a: Science seeks to understand nature (why?); engineering seeks to change the world by applying knowledge to make things work (how?).

anki.q: How does Petroski characterize the scientist/engineer difference?
anki.a: Scientists prize publication and peer recognition; engineers value things that work. They are trained differently and often misunderstand each other.

anki.q: Which is the broader term: engineering or technology?
anki.a: Technology — it encompasses all human-made tools and techniques. Engineering is a formalized subset that applies scientific principles with mathematical analysis under economic constraints.

anki.q: Give an example of technology that is NOT engineering.
anki.a: Traditional crafts, vernacular (folk) architecture, or folk medicine — technology developed without formal engineering methods.

anki.q: What multiple obligations does the professional engineer face?
anki.a: Obligations to employers, clients, the public, and the engineering profession itself — these can create ethical conflicts.

anki.q: Why does Davis think studying the history of engineering ethics is important?
anki.a: It shows how ethical obligations arose and how engineers have navigated (or failed to navigate) conflicts between competing duties.

anki.q: Who is Henry Petroski and what is he known for?
anki.a: A civil engineer and prolific author (To Engineer Is Human) who writes about engineering for general audiences; famous for analyzing design and failure.

anki.q: What does 'engineering as professional practice' mean?
anki.a: Engineering is a social practice embedded in institutions and ethical norms — not just a technical skill set. Ethics is intrinsic, not added on.

anki.q: Why are engineering's boundaries difficult to define?
anki.a: Because engineering overlaps with science (uses scientific knowledge), technology (a subset of it), and crafts (shares hands-on making).

anki.q: What is a 'conflict of interest' for an engineer?
anki.a: When the engineer's obligations to employer, client, and public tension — e.g., employer wants a cheaper design that raises public safety risks.

anki.q: What does Petroski's 'Scientists vs. Engineers' essay argue?
anki.a: That scientists and engineers have fundamentally different values and goals, often misunderstood by both groups and the public.

anki.q: By Week 2, what conceptual framework does the course want students to understand?
anki.a: That engineering is a distinct profession (not just technology or science), with its own history, ethics, social context, and boundaries — a framework applied throughout the course.

quiz.q: According to Davis, what is the defining feature that makes engineering a 'profession'?
options: A shared ethical code of conduct
quiz.explanation: Davis argues that a code of shared ethical standards — not just technical expertise — is what distinguishes a profession.

quiz.q: When scientists and engineers interact, what key value difference does Petroski highlight?
options: Engineers value theory; scientists value practice
Scientists value publication; engineers value things that work
Engineers value money; scientists value truth
Scientists prefer teamwork; engineers prefer solo work
quiz.explanation: Petroski notes scientists prize peer recognition and publication while engineers prize functional outcomes.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the BROADEST term?
quiz.explanation: Technology is the broadest category — it encompasses all human-made tools and techniques; engineering is a formal subset of it.

quiz.q: What year was the ASCE founded?
quiz.explanation: The ASCE was founded in 1852, making it one of the earliest formal professional engineering organizations in the U.S.

quiz.q: Which scenario represents a classic professional conflict of interest for an engineer?
options: Choosing which programming language to use
Employer wants a cheaper design that raises public safety risks
Deciding between two equally safe materials
quiz.explanation: Conflicts arise when employer interests (cost, speed) clash with the engineer's obligation to protect public safety.
